cells.tense: The strands are coming together right now and your hand is the one on the pen.
cells.ask: Say out loud the two things you are holding apart. Then say which one the next hour belongs to.
cells.core:
You are carrying more than one thing at once and it has not cost you your shape. Nothing got dropped, nothing got jammed into an order it does not fit. You hold the whole load the way you hold something that has to stay level, shifting your weight as it shifts. What you decide, you decide from what is actually in front of you.

The fairness under it runs without grinding. You give what is owed and take what is yours and you are not keeping score, which is what keeps your grip clean. The pressure has not made you stiff and it has not made you spill. You are still in the room with the people inside this while you carry it. Keep the pen where it is.
cells.sheetLine: You hold the strands together and you pick the order.

cells.tense: You are bracing for a scene that has not happened and your hands are already on it.
cells.ask: Take the outcome you keep rehearsing and write beside it what you will do if it does not come. Ten minutes, then put it down.
cells.core:
You are gathering things that have not scattered yet. Every position gets mapped early, every version of how it could go gets held in advance, and the assembly turns into bracing. A chunk of what you are carrying is weight nobody handed you. The pressure is mostly from a future that does not arrive to be settled, so it keeps its hold.

The endurance underneath is real, just pointed the wrong way. More strength is not what this needs. It needs direction that comes from what you actually feel, not from what you have already decided you will have to survive. When the motion starts from real engagement, the load gets lighter on its own — not because you set it down, but because you quit lifting it ahead of time.

cells.tense: The pulling of the strands into one line stopped a while ago and you have stood at that door since.
cells.ask: Sit with one person you trust and say one thing you have been carrying alone. Not to fix it, just to have it heard.
cells.core:
You stopped gathering. The strands did not leave. They are still there, still yours, but the work of pulling them into one line stopped somewhere behind you, and you have been standing in front of that closed door ever since. You know what the carrying takes and you have not been able to make yourself take it up again, so the load sits where it fell.

What is missing is not strength. It is the settled sense of being in contact, with yourself and with someone who knows you. That quiet connection is what refills your capacity to hold, not trying harder at it. You do not have to pick the whole load up today. You only have to stop standing alone in the doorway.
cells.sheetLine: The load is still there and you stopped picking it up.

cells.tense: You are already writing how this ends and telling it as if someone else held the pen.
cells.ask: Name one thing you did to keep this together, say it was your call, and tell one person what you decided and why.
cells.core:
You have been holding this together for a while — strands gathered, order chosen, weight carried — and you describe it as something that happened to you, or that the situation forced, or that just needed doing. The hand on the pen has been yours the whole time. The calls that made this coherent were calls, and you made them.

The strength in it is not something you were handed. It is something you are doing. Say it in your own name and it can travel. The people around you can learn from how you hold things, and you can keep holding without shrinking what it takes from you.
cells.sheetLine: You've been holding this together and calling it nobody's doing.
